Question three. Compare Parquet, ORC, and Avro. Parquet and ORC, optimized row columnar, are both columnar and compressed, with per-column statistics that let a reader skip data. Parquet is the default nearly every engine reads; ORC grew up around Hive, in the Hadoop world. Avro, a row-based binary format, writes whole records, and its files carry the schema they were written with. It suits streaming, one record at a time, often on Kafka, a distributed log, and its compatibility rules let a schema evolve. And over CSV, Parquet carries types and a schema, and here it's under a quarter of the size. Columnar for analytics, Avro for records in motion.

Question four. Why is compression more effective in columnar formats? A column holds one type, often with few distinct values. Region has four. Parquet writes each one once, in a dictionary, then about three bits a row: a million regions in three hundred eighty kilobytes, against five and a half megabytes of text. Amount is random to the cent, so it only shrinks from six point eight megabytes to four point two. Sorting before writing makes long runs. In date order, a million dates take three kilobytes. Sorted by region, the region column falls to five hundred fifty-four bytes. Codecs trade too. Zstandard wrote this table in six point three megabytes, Snappy, the default, in nine point four, but Zstandard decompresses slower. Over a slow link the smaller file wins; on a fast disk, the faster codec.
